title: Summit and font (Sacrosanctum Concilium 10)
hookLine: the liturgy is the summit toward which everything moves and its source
tomorrow: the priest does the praying. so what's left for the pew?

cards: Sunday night can feel like the top of something, and Monday at seven a.m. like the bottom of a well.
A mountain has two well-known places: the peak everyone climbs toward, and the spring somewhere on its slope where the river begins. Usually they're different spots.
Sacrosanctum Concilium, the council's document on the liturgy, says that in the Church's life they're the same place.

teach.b: Start with a careful step the council takes just before. Paragraph nine says the liturgy doesn't exhaust everything the Church does: there's preaching, conversion, works of love.
So paragraph ten isn't saying nothing else matters.

teach.h: THE SUMMIT: WHERE IT ALL HEADS.
teach.b: It's saying where everything is headed. That's the summit.

All the Church's work, the paragraph says, aims at this: that people made children of God by faith and baptism come together, praise God in the midst of the Church, take part in the sacrifice, and eat the Lord's supper.
The soup kitchen and the catechism class both point uphill, toward that gathering. Now the font.
The same liturgy is where the Church's strength flows from. From the liturgy, and above all the Eucharist, grace pours out, the council says, as from a fountain.
People leave Mass and go back down the mountain carrying water.
Put the two together and you get a loop, not a ladder.
The week flows toward the altar, and the altar sends the week back out, and then the week climbs back up. Last, why the council bothered to say it.
The paragraph ties the liturgy to living: those fed by these sacraments are urged to be one in holiness and to hold on, in their lives, to what they've received in faith.

how: Catholics gather for Mass on Sundays and holy days, and some go during the week; parishes often describe their outreach and teaching as flowing from, and leading back to, the Mass.

o: the liturgy as the Church's peak and its spring
a church's bell tower and its baptism bowl
a mountain shrine where pilgrims are baptized

games.q: the peak and the spring — tap the pairs.
p: where the Church's work is headed
grace pours out, as from a fountain

s: the council says the liturgy is the only thing the Church does
paragraph nine says it doesn't exhaust the Church's activity: preaching, conversion, works of love.
the council calls the liturgy both summit and font
the peak the Church's work climbs toward, and the spring its strength flows from.
if Mass really worked, one time would be enough
it's a loop: the week flows toward the altar, and the altar sends the week back out.

games.q: your friend volunteers at a shelter every Saturday and says that's her real worship, so she's dropping Mass. by paragraphs nine and ten, what's the honest reply?
o: the council prizes that work, and says it heads toward the liturgy and flows from it.
the shelter doesn't count; the council says only Mass matters.
the council says Mass is optional for people who serve the poor.
games.why: paragraph nine says the liturgy doesn't exhaust the Church's activity; paragraph ten says that activity climbs toward the liturgy and draws its strength from it.

practice: Make a small plan in three steps. Name one gathering where you're fed and sent back out: Mass this week if you go, or another place if you don't.
Name what usually gets in the way, then one small move that clears it, and rest on that plan until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Summit and font. The council's picture of the liturgy: the peak the Church's life climbs toward, and the spring it flows from. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin in Sacrosanctum Concilium 10: the liturgy is the summit and the font.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: summit and font, uphill to the altar and back down carrying water. See you tomorrow.

sources.work: Second Vatican Council, Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy
